lesson.title: Performing Under Watchful Eyes
lesson.summary: The tendency for the presence of other people to improve performance on simple or well practiced tasks while impairing performance on complex or unfamiliar ones.
lesson.body:
Social facilitation is one of the oldest documented findings in social psychology, and it captures a genuinely two sided effect. When other people are present, whether as an audience or as co-actors doing the same task nearby, performance on tasks a person already knows well tends to improve, while performance on tasks that are new, complex, or not yet mastered tends to get worse. Both halves of this pattern connect back to social norms, since the mere presence of others carries an implicit social evaluation, an awareness that one's performance might be judged, that changes how people perform even when no one says a word.

The effect was first documented in 1898 by Norman Triplett, often credited with running one of the very first true experiments in social psychology. Triplett had noticed that competitive cyclists posted faster race times when riding against other cyclists than when riding alone against a clock, and he confirmed a version of the effect in a simple lab task involving a fishing reel wound as quickly as possible, alone or alongside another person doing the same task.

The most influential explanation came from Robert Zajonc in 1965, whose drive theory proposed that the mere presence of others increases physiological arousal, and that heightened arousal makes a person's dominant response, the response that comes most naturally or automatically, more likely to occur. For a simple or well learned task, the dominant response is usually the correct one, so arousal helps. For a complex or unfamiliar task, the dominant response is often a mistake, so arousal hurts. Zajonc and colleagues extended the idea beyond humans in a 1969 study finding that cockroaches ran a simple, straight runway faster when other cockroaches were present as an audience, but took longer to solve a more complex maze under the same audience conditions, suggesting the basic mechanism does not require complex social reasoning to occur.

Later researchers proposed refinements rather than replacements for Zajonc's account. Evaluation apprehension theory suggests that arousal in the presence of others depends specifically on the sense that one's performance is being judged, not mere physical presence alone, which is why an inattentive or non evaluative audience tends to produce weaker facilitation effects than an attentive, evaluative one. Distraction conflict theory offers a related idea, that others draw attention away from the task itself, and this conflict between attending to others and attending to the task is what drives arousal. These explanations are not fully settled or mutually exclusive, but together they explain why the presence of others is not a simple boost or drain, it depends heavily on what the task demands and how being watched is experienced.
